The strongest result is a reduction in the depth of feedback

I pursued this capability: construct an experiment that matches unrestricted adaptive planning without constructing the adaptive policy—and retain useful feedback with only one decision between measurement batches.

For a known quadratic target under a known Gaussian input law, I obtained an explicit construction with the following guarantee:

At most

k+1 exact scalar linear measurements, arranged in two rounds, achieve no greater squared prediction error than any adaptive policy using 
𝑘
k measurements.

The comparison also covers policies with an expected budget of 
𝑘
k. A separate noisy result establishes a substantial difference in final accuracy against the optimal fixed experiment, including repeated and nonorthogonal measurements.

This changes the measurement interface: the central construction permits programmable linear functionals of the unknown input. I kept that resource explicit and developed a separate companion for the original coordinate-only interface.

The completed deliverables are:

p1_two_round_measurement.pdf — the 13-page research note, with ordinary proofs, acquisition and precision bounds, cost accounting, results, and primary comparisons.
p1_two_round_evidence.zip — executable constructions, six replayed evidence sets, two independent internal proof reviews, acquisition and coordinate companions, source ledger, useful failures, and a factual handoff to the preceding work.

The previous residual-risk theorem, sharper quadratic bound, rare-concentration obstruction, acquisition constructions, and corrections remain unchanged. I checked the preceding bundle’s manifest. No repository integration was performed.

1. The organizing mechanism: make the remaining target easy to measure

The important choice is what the first measurements should accomplish.

For a nonlinear target, a measurement can have little immediate predictive value while revealing which later measurement would be valuable. The rare-gate construction already exposed this phenomenon. Here it leads to a constructive strategy:

Choose a first batch that removes much of the nonlinear dependence on the unobserved input.
Use its outcomes to identify the remaining linear functional.
Measure that functional directly.
